Filter to your zone so the board becomes a usable task list, and know how to un-filter instantly when a code is called elsewhere
quiz.why: A 38-row board is unreadable, so the filtered view is what makes orders and results actionable. A printed board goes stale within minutes and creates a privacy risk, and depending on someone else to filter it wastes their time daily.

quiz.q: The board shows a patient marked 'admitted-boarding' in room 22 for the last five hours. What is your responsibility?
choices: None; the patient belongs to the inpatient team now
Continue routine care: vitals on the ordered schedule, toileting, repositioning, meals and hygiene
Vitals only, since the ED workup is finished
Transport them to the floor without waiting for a bed assignment
quiz.why: A boarded patient is physically yours until they leave the department, and boarders are the patients most often neglected because the team has mentally filed them as finished. Nothing may be transported anywhere without an assigned bed and a report.

quiz.q: A 4-year-old's chart shows a weight of 42 in a field labeled kg. What is the risk, and what do you do?
choices: It is almost certainly a pounds value in a kilogram field, which would roughly double weight-based doses; tell the nurse and get a scale weight in kilograms
No risk, since providers double-check all doses
Convert it to 19 kg yourself and update the field
Leave it and note your concern in the flowsheet comments
quiz.why: A typical 4-year-old is roughly 16 to 18 kg, so 42 is a pounds value, and every milligram-per-kilogram dose calculated from it is more than double. Silent conversion substitutes your arithmetic for a measurement, and a comment nobody reads does not stop an order.

quiz.q: Before entering a room to draw blood, which set of chart facts should you check?
choices: Insurance, provider, and disposition
Chief complaint and prior visits
Allergies, code status, isolation precautions, and weight
The provider's note and the triage narrative
quiz.why: Those four change what you may do and what you must wear: latex allergy affects gloves and tourniquets, isolation dictates personal protective equipment, and code status must be known before an event rather than during one. The others are useful context but do not change the task's safety.

quiz.q: You perform a 12-lead EKG on a chest pain patient at 2106 and hand it to the physician at 2107, but you never document it in the system. What are the two consequences?
choices: None, because the physician received the tracing
The order stays open so another tech may repeat it, and the door-to-EKG clock never stops, showing the department as non-compliant
The tracing is deleted from the chart automatically
The nurse is required to document it on your behalf
quiz.why: Documentation is what closes the order and stops the metric clock, which is calculated from arrival time to the charted acquisition time. Tracings are not deleted, and a nurse cannot chart work she did not perform.

quiz.q: An order for a urine specimen has been open for 90 minutes because the patient cannot void. Nobody has been told. What was the correct action at the point you knew?
choices: Cancel the order and let the provider reorder if needed
Wait, since the patient will eventually be able to give a sample
Document it at the end of the shift with the reason
Tell the nurse and document it as unable to obtain with the reason, so the team can offer fluids, wait, or catheterize
quiz.why: An open order with no explanation stalls a workup invisibly while a provider waits on a urinalysis. Techs do not cancel provider orders, and end-of-shift documentation is 90 minutes too late to change any decision.

quiz.q: You obtained vital signs at 2105 and are charting them at 2140 after helping with a code. Which entry is correct?
choices: Enter them in a column timed 2105, marked as a late entry per policy
Enter them in a column timed 2140, the time of documentation
Enter them at 2140 and add a comment that they were taken earlier
Retake vitals and chart only the new set
quiz.why: Every reader assumes the column time is the measurement time, and sepsis, stroke and deterioration decisions are made from those times. A comment does not fix a wrong timestamp, and discarding a real measurement erases a data point in a trend.

quiz.q: Which documented oxygen saturation is most clinically useful?
choices: SpO2 94 percent
SpO2 94 percent on 4 L nasal cannula
SpO2 adequate
SpO2 94 percent, patient comfortable
quiz.why: The same saturation means very different things on room air versus supplemental oxygen, so delivery is part of the measurement. A bare number is ambiguous, 'adequate' is a conclusion rather than data, and comfort is a separate observation.

quiz.q: A patient in violent restraints has a restraint flowsheet with checks at 1400, 1415, 1500, and 1515. What does an auditor conclude?
choices: Documentation is complete
Documentation is adequate because checks resumed
The 1430 and 1445 checks are missing, which is a documented monitoring gap and a regulatory finding
Only the provider's face-to-face evaluation matters
quiz.why: Most hospital policies operationalize continuous monitoring of violent restraint as a documented check every 15 minutes, so a 45-minute interval is a gap regardless of whether the patient was actually observed. The face-to-face evaluation is a separate additional requirement, not a substitute.

quiz.q: Which EKG entry is documented correctly by a technician?
choices: EKG completed and left at the desk for review.
EKG obtained 2106, rate 118, no acute ST changes.
EKG obtained 2106, 12-lead, handed to Dr. Rivera 2107.
EKG done this shift.
quiz.why: It records the acquisition time and the handoff to a named provider, which closes the loop and stops the door-to-EKG clock. Leaving it at a desk is not a handoff, interpretation is outside the tech scope, and an entry without a time is not usable data.

quiz.q: You apply a volar splint to a right wrist and document what was applied and the patient's instructions. Which required element is missing?
choices: Neurovascular status documented both before and after application
The manufacturer of the splint material
The provider's signature on the splint order
The patient's pain score at discharge
quiz.why: The pre- and post-application checks of pulse, motor function, sensation and capillary refill are the evidence the limb was perfused when you finished, which is how a too-tight splint is caught early. Materials and signatures do not protect the limb.

quiz.q: A patient has had three unsuccessful venipuncture attempts by two different techs, but only the first tech documented attempts. What is the practical risk?
choices: None, since the blood will eventually be obtained
A third operator will attempt blindly rather than escalating to ultrasound guidance or vascular access, because the record understates the attempts
The patient will be billed twice
The specimen will be rejected by the lab
quiz.why: Attempt counts exist to trigger escalation and cap repeated sticks, so an undercounted record produces more unnecessary needles in an already difficult patient. Billing and specimen acceptance are unaffected by attempt documentation.

quiz.q: A tech draws two tubes, is pulled to help lift a patient, and labels the tubes at the workstation four minutes later with labels he is certain are correct. What is the required action?
choices: Send them, since the identity is certain
Send them with a note documenting the delay
Discard them and recollect after re-verifying identity at the bedside
Send them for chemistry but recollect for blood bank
quiz.why: Certainty is exactly what every mislabeling event felt like at the time; labeling must occur at the bedside because that is the only moment identity can be verified. A note does not restore a broken identity link, and the standard is not relaxed for non-blood-bank tests.

quiz.q: A sepsis protocol fires at triage: lactate, blood cultures, and antibiotics are ordered. The nurse is ready with the antibiotic and you have not yet drawn the cultures. What should happen?
choices: Give the antibiotic first, since time to antibiotics is the measured metric
Draw cultures only if the patient has a documented fever
Skip cultures and rely on the urine culture instead
Draw the blood cultures first, then the antibiotic goes in
quiz.why: One antibiotic dose can sterilize the sample and eliminate the organism identification that guides days of therapy. Fever is not required to draw cultures, and a urine culture does not substitute for blood cultures in suspected bacteremia.

quiz.q: A nurse in another room asks you to chart on the MAR that she administered acetaminophen. What is the correct action?
choices: Chart it with a comment identifying her as the administering nurse
Decline; medication documentation belongs to the licensed person who performed the checks and the barcode scan
Chart it and notify the charge nurse afterward
Chart it in the flowsheet instead of the MAR
quiz.why: Medication documentation is tied to the person who verified the five rights and scanned the patient and drug, so any tech entry breaks that chain and is falsification of a legal record. Moving it to a flowsheet does not change what it is.

quiz.q: You run a point-of-care glucose on a drowsy 71-year-old and the meter reads 34 mg/dL. What is the correct first action?
choices: Find the nurse immediately and report the value in person
Repeat the test on the other hand to confirm before reporting
Chart the value and finish your remaining rooms
Give the patient juice while you look for the nurse
quiz.why: A glucose of 34 with altered mental status is a treatable emergency in minutes. Repeating first delays treatment, charting alone alerts no one, and anything by mouth in a drowsy patient risks aspiration and is not a tech decision.

quiz.q: While checking results you see a potassium of 7.1 flagged critical on a patient in your zone. The nurse is at the desk. What do you do?
choices: Assume the lab has already called the nurse
Send it by secure chat so there is a written record
Tell the nurse in person right now, without assuming the lab's call has landed
Tell the provider and let them tell the nurse
quiz.why: A potassium of 7.1 threatens a lethal rhythm, and laboratory notification can be delayed or reach someone off the unit. In-person notification to the assigned nurse is the reliable channel; a chat message can sit unread, and routing through a third person adds delay.

quiz.q: A patient you checked 20 minutes ago is now pale, diaphoretic, and answering slowly. Which communication is appropriate?
choices: Secure chat to the nurse, then continue your task list
Chart the change in the flowsheet and wait for rounds
Page the provider through the messaging system
Get the nurse in person immediately, or call out for help from the room
quiz.why: A visibly changed patient is an emergent escalation, and chat and paging can both sit unanswered for many minutes. Charting is necessary but is not a way of alerting anyone, and waiting for rounds forfeits the time that matters.

quiz.q: A stroke protocol has fired for a 68-year-old with sudden left-sided weakness. Which tech task comes first?
choices: Point-of-care glucose, because hypoglycemia mimics stroke and is corrected in minutes
A 12-lead EKG
A full set of vital signs including temperature
Transport to CT before any bedside testing
quiz.why: Hypoglycemia imitates a stroke perfectly and is reversed in two minutes, so it is excluded first before a patient is committed to a thrombolysis pathway. The EKG, full vitals, and CT all follow immediately but do not precede the glucose.

quiz.q: Which documentation entry by a tech is written correctly?
choices: Patient uncooperative and clearly exaggerating pain.
Patient stated, 'I don't want anyone touching my arm right now.' Nurse notified at 1420.
Patient appears intoxicated; incident report completed.
Wound appears infected, dressing changed.
quiz.why: A direct quote plus an action and a time is verifiable fact. The others state conclusions about motive and diagnosis, and referencing an incident report pulls a protected quality document into the legal medical record.

quiz.q: Which of these may appear in a medical record?
choices: .25 mg
MSO4 4 mg
quiz.why: A leading zero prevents a missed decimal point being read as 25 mg. A missing leading zero and a trailing zero are both on the do-not-use list because of documented tenfold overdoses, and MSO4 has been confused with magnesium sulfate.

quiz.q: The EHR is down for three hours. Vital signs are recorded on paper downtime forms. When the system returns, how should those entries be handled?
choices: Filed as paper in the physical chart with no electronic entry
Entered with the recovery time, since that is when the system received them
Back-entered with the original times each measurement was taken
Summarized in one note describing the downtime
quiz.why: Back-entry with original times preserves the true clinical sequence that every audit and downstream decision depends on. Entry times falsify the timeline, and a summary destroys the individual measurements the record requires.

quiz.q: A tech realizes at 0500 that he never charted the 0300 restraint check, although he performed it. What is the correct action?
choices: Document it now as a late entry with the actual 0300 observation time, per policy
Backdate the entry to 0300 with no notation
Leave it blank, since a late entry draws attention
Chart it at 0500 as if the check occurred then
quiz.why: Late entries are permitted and expected; the record needs the real observation time plus an indication that it was entered later. Silent backdating and charting a false observation time are both falsification, and a blank check is a regulatory finding on its own.

quiz.q: A patient's board row shows a contact precautions icon. You are going in to take vital signs. What is the sequence?
choices: Take the vitals quickly and wash hands thoroughly afterward
Perform hand hygiene and put on gown and gloves before entering, then remove them and perform hand hygiene before leaving
Put on gloves at the bedside once you see what you are dealing with
Gown only if the patient has visible drainage
quiz.why: Contact precautions require the personal protective equipment to be on before contact with the room environment, not after touching the bed rail, and removed inside the room. Deciding at the bedside or based on visible drainage means the exposure has already happened.

quiz.q: An order reads 'vital signs every 15 minutes.' Reviewing the flowsheet you find columns at 1300, 1315, 1400, and 1415. What is the most accurate statement?
choices: The record is acceptable because the frequency resumed
The gap is acceptable if the patient was stable
The 1330 and 1345 intervals are missing, which is a documented gap and the first thing found in any case review
The nurse is responsible for the gap, not the tech
quiz.why: An ordered frequency must appear as columns at that frequency; stability is a conclusion drawn from measurements that were never taken. Responsibility follows the assignment, and in most departments timed vitals are the tech's.

quiz.q: You are transporting a patient to CT. What belongs in the transport documentation?
choices: Only the destination
Nothing; transport is not a documented event
The provider who ordered the imaging
Departure time, destination, who accompanied the patient, what monitoring went along, and return time
quiz.why: Patients deteriorate in elevators and corridors, and the transport record is the only evidence of who was present and what was being watched. Destination alone cannot establish supervision, and the ordering provider is already recorded on the order.

quiz.q: An alert but hard-of-hearing patient is about to have blood drawn. Which identification method is acceptable?
choices: Read the name and date of birth from the wristband and ask the patient to nod if correct
Ask the patient to state their full name and date of birth, then compare to the wristband
Confirm the room number against the tracking board
Ask the family member at the bedside to confirm the patient's identity
quiz.why: Hard-of-hearing, confused and sedated patients agree to names that are not theirs, which is exactly how mislabeled specimens begin. Room numbers change constantly in an ED, and a family member's confirmation is not one of the two required identifiers.

quiz.q: A tech wants to become fast in Epic in the first month. Which approach is most effective?
choices: Practice in the training environment, collect the educator's tip sheets, and ask the designated super-users, while learning the column time field, board filters, and how to mark a task unable to obtain
Ask the busiest nurse in the department each time something is unclear
Learn only the screens needed for the current assignment and avoid the rest
Watch a colleague chart without touching the system until orientation ends
quiz.why: A training environment lets errors happen harmlessly, tip sheets and super-users exist specifically for this, and those three functions cover most of a shift. Interrupting the busiest nurse burns goodwill, avoidance guarantees slow charting, and passive watching does not build the motor habits.

scenarios.title: One patient, charted right
scenarios.intro:
1902. You have just taken report for zone B. The track board shows a new row: room 9, Alvarez, 58-year-old male, ESI 2, chief complaint 'chest pressure,' arrival time 1857, no provider assigned yet. Two icons next to the name: a fall risk band and an allergy alert.

The Orders column already shows three items. Triage started the chest pain protocol: 12-lead EKG, point-of-care glucose, and a full set of labs with troponin. All are marked STAT.

The door-to-EKG target is 10 minutes from arrival. The clock started at 1857.

steps.prompt: You are standing at the workstation with the board open. What is the first thing you do?

choices.text: Acknowledge the EKG order, glance at the Storyboard for allergies, code status and isolation, and walk to room 9 with the machine.
choices.feedback: Correct on both counts. Acknowledging claims the task so a second tech does not duplicate it, and the ten-second header check costs nothing and tells you what you are walking into.

choices.text: Go straight to the room with the EKG machine without touching the board, since the clock is running.
choices.feedback: The urgency instinct is right and the shortcut is not. An unacknowledged order invites a duplicate EKG, and you are walking in blind to an allergy alert you already saw an icon for.

choices.text: Read the triage note in full, then the prior visits in Chart Review, to understand the history before you go in.
choices.feedback: You have just spent four minutes of a ten-minute target reading. On an ESI 2 chest pain the EKG comes first; history can be read while the tracing prints.

choices.text: Draw the labs first since you are already near the supply cart, then do the EKG.
choices.feedback: Both are ordered, but only one has a ten-minute clock attached and only one identifies a heart attack that needs a catheterization lab activated. EKG first, always, on chest pain.

steps.prompt: You are at the bedside. The patient is diaphoretic and holding his chest. He confirms his name and date of birth. You acquire a clean 12-lead at 1904.

choices.text: Carry the tracing directly to the nearest physician or PA, hand it to them, and note their name and the time.
choices.feedback: This is the entire point of the task. The clock stops when a provider has it in their hands, and the name and time are what you will document.

choices.text: Place the tracing in the provider rack at the desk and start on the labs.
choices.feedback: A rack is storage, not a handoff. An ST elevation sitting in a rack for nine minutes is precisely how an infarct gets missed, and the metric counts the handoff, not the acquisition.

choices.text: Look at the tracing yourself first; if it looks normal, finish your other rooms and hand it over after.
choices.feedback: Interpretation is outside your scope and beside the point. Even an experienced tech's read is not a clinical decision, and a delay based on your own reassurance is the worst version of the rack problem.

choices.text: Show it to the patient's nurse first, and let her take it to the provider.
choices.feedback: Telling the nurse is right and routing through her adds a step to a ten-minute clock. Hand it to a provider directly, then tell the nurse it is done and what time.

steps.prompt: Dr. Okafor takes the tracing at 1905, glances at it, and says 'sinus tach, no elevation, thanks.' You are back at the workstation. How do you document the EKG?

choices.text: EKG done, given to provider.
choices.feedback: No times and no name. This entry proves nothing, stops no clock, and will show in an audit as a missed door-to-EKG even though you hit it by three minutes.

choices.text: EKG obtained 1904, 12-lead, handed to Dr. Okafor 1905.
choices.feedback: Exactly right: what, when acquired, and when handed to a named provider. Seven minutes from a 1857 arrival, and the record proves it.

choices.text: EKG obtained 1904, 12-lead, sinus tachycardia at 104, no ST elevation, handed to Dr. Okafor 1905.
choices.feedback: The structure is right and the interpretation does not belong to you, even when you are repeating the physician's words. Document what you did; the provider documents what it showed.

choices.text: EKG obtained 1904, handed to provider 1905.
choices.feedback: Close, and the missing piece is which provider. In a department with four clinicians on, 'provider' does not identify anyone, and this is the line that establishes a physician saw the tracing.

steps.prompt: Next: the labs and the point-of-care glucose. You are in the room with the patient, the labels are printed at the bedside printer, and you have scanned his wristband. You draw four tubes at 1913 from the left antecubital, first attempt.

choices.text: Label all four tubes at the bedside in front of him, scan each label, mark the specimens collected at 1913, and run the glucose while you are still in the room.
choices.feedback: Every step in the right order. Labeling in the room in front of the patient is the only moment identity can be verified, and doing the glucose before you leave saves a second trip.

choices.text: Carry the tubes and labels to the workstation where there is more counter space, label them there, and scan them in.
choices.feedback: A tube that leaves the room unlabeled has no verifiable identity link. Every large mislabeling event in the literature starts exactly here, with a reasonable-sounding convenience.

choices.text: Label the tubes at the bedside but mark them collected later when you get back to the workstation, using the current time.
choices.feedback: The labeling is right and the timestamp is wrong. Collection time is a clinical data point, especially for a troponin that will be repeated on an interval measured from this draw.

choices.text: Pre-label the tubes before the draw so the labels do not get mixed up mid-procedure.
choices.feedback: Pre-labeling empty tubes is prohibited everywhere. If the draw fails or you move to another patient, you are holding labeled tubes with no verified contents, which is the mislabel waiting to happen.

steps.prompt: 1918. The glucose meter reads 212 mg/dL. The order set also includes vital signs every 15 minutes. You took the set at 1903 that is already charted. What now?

choices.text: Chart the glucose, tell the nurse the value, and set yourself to retake vitals at 1918, charting each set at the time it was taken.
choices.feedback: Right. A glucose of 212 is not critical but it is a finding the nurse needs, and a q15 order means a flowsheet column every 15 minutes starting from the first one.

choices.text: Chart the glucose and wait for the nurse to ask about it, since 212 is not a critical value.
choices.feedback: Correct that it is not critical and wrong that silence is acceptable. Telling the nurse takes four seconds and is how a tech becomes someone whose work does not have to be checked.

choices.text: Chart the glucose and take the next vitals at the top of the hour so the columns are tidy.
choices.feedback: The order says every 15 minutes, not on the hour. Tidiness is not a clinical standard, and a 1903 to 2000 gap is a documented miss on an ESI 2 chest pain.

choices.text: Repeat the glucose on the other hand to verify before charting anything.
choices.feedback: Repeat confirmation is for implausible or off-scale readings. A 212 in a diaphoretic 58-year-old is entirely plausible, and a second stick is an unnecessary needle.

steps.prompt: 1946. Dr. Okafor orders a chest x-ray in radiology, so the patient leaves the department. He is on a monitor and has a fall risk band. You are taking him.

choices.text: Check the MAR before you go, take him with monitoring and the nurse's awareness, and chart departure time, destination, who went, what monitoring, and return time.
choices.feedback: The MAR check is the part new techs skip: a patient who just received nitroglycerin or an opioid can drop a pressure in a hallway. Everything else here is the standard transport record.

choices.text: Take him down and chart the transport when you get back, with the times you remember.
choices.feedback: Your memory for exact times is reliable for about ten minutes. Note the departure time before you leave, even on your hand, then chart real numbers rather than approximations.

choices.text: Take him down quickly without telling the nurse; she can see on the board that he is off the unit.
choices.feedback: The board updates only if someone updates it, and a nurse looking for her chest pain patient during a hallway deterioration is a serious problem. Tell her, every time.

choices.text: Leave the monitor behind since radiology is two minutes away and the equipment is awkward in the elevator.
choices.feedback: A monitored chest pain patient stays monitored. The two minutes in the elevator are exactly where an unwitnessed rhythm change happens, and the transport record would then show nobody was watching.

scenarios.debrief:
One patient, six tasks, and every one of them had the same three-part shape: acknowledge it, do it, document it with the real time and tell the nurse.

The door-to-EKG clock is the clearest example of documentation being the work rather than paperwork about the work. You acquired at 1904 and handed off at 1905 from a 1857 arrival, which is eight minutes, and none of that exists unless the entry names the time and the provider. 'EKG done, given to provider' would have recorded a compliant department as non-compliant and left no proof a physician saw the tracing.

The specimen sequence has exactly one non-negotiable step: the tube is labeled in the room, in front of the patient, before you leave. Convenience is how every mislabeling event begins.

Two habits to carry out of this case. Read the Storyboard for ten seconds before every room, and check the MAR before you move a patient anywhere. Both cost nothing and both prevent the kind of error that is impossible to explain afterward.

scenarios.title: The tube that went out wrong
scenarios.intro:
0338 on a night shift. Twenty minutes ago you drew blood on two patients in adjacent rooms: room 3, a 44-year-old woman with abdominal pain, and room 4, a 61-year-old man with weakness and a history of kidney disease. Both sets went up the tube system together.

You are restocking the supply cart when you remember the sequence and something does not sit right. You pull up room 4's chart. The specimen collection entry says the tubes were collected at 0316, which matches. Then you look at the label stock still sitting on the counter by room 3's door: one unused label with room 4's patient name on it.

You drew room 4's blood using labels you carried in with you. And you are now not sure which patient's labels went on which tubes.

steps.prompt: Your stomach drops. The tubes are already in the lab. What is your first action?

choices.text: Call the lab immediately and ask them to hold or discard both patients' specimens, then tell the nurses and the charge nurse.
choices.feedback: First and fastest. The only thing that matters in this minute is stopping a result from posting to the wrong chart, because once it posts, someone may act on it.

choices.text: Go to the lab in person to sort out which tube is which and correct the labels there.
choices.feedback: Relabeling destroys any ability to prove which blood came from which person, so the specimens are worthless regardless. It also converts a recoverable error into a falsification problem.

choices.text: Wait to see whether the results come back plausible for each patient before raising it.
choices.feedback: Plausibility is not identity. A potassium that looks reasonable for the wrong patient is exactly how a wrong-patient result gets believed and acted on.

choices.text: Tell your preceptor first and ask what to do.
choices.feedback: Telling someone is far better than saying nothing, and it is one step slower than it needs to be. Call the lab, then tell everyone, and the two together take under a minute.

steps.prompt: The lab tech says one specimen is still in the queue and can be discarded, but the chemistry panel on the tube labeled for room 4 has already resulted. Two minutes ago.

choices.text: Tell the nurse and the provider for room 4 right now that the resulted chemistry may not be his blood and must not be acted on.
choices.feedback: This is the emergency inside the error. A man with kidney disease has a potassium on his screen that may belong to someone else, and a treatment decision could be made on it in the next few minutes.

choices.text: Ask the lab to retract the result from the chart so nobody sees it.
choices.feedback: Asking the lab to correct the record is part of the process, but it takes time and the provider may be looking at that value right now. A human being has to be told before a system change is made.

choices.text: Recollect from both patients first so replacement results are on the way before you raise it.
choices.feedback: Recollection is necessary and it is not first. Every minute a suspect potassium sits on a renal patient's chart unflagged is a minute someone might treat it.

choices.text: Document the error in the chart so the team sees it when they open the record.
choices.feedback: Passive notification is not notification. Documentation is required, and it reaches people minutes or hours later, which is the wrong speed for a result that is on a screen now.

steps.prompt: The provider says nothing was acted on. The result is flagged and retracted by the lab. The charge nurse asks you to recollect both patients. Room 3 is annoyed: 'You already took my blood.'

choices.text: "You're right, and I'm sorry. There was a labeling problem with the samples, so we can't use them and I need to redraw to be sure the results are yours. I'll use the other arm."
choices.feedback: Honest, brief, no jargon, no blame, and no over-explaining. Patients accept a redraw far more easily when they are told the truth plainly than when they are given a vague reason.

choices.text: "The lab rejected the sample, it happens sometimes."
choices.feedback: It is a deflection onto the lab and it is not what happened. If she later learns the real reason, everything else you have told her becomes suspect.

choices.text: "I need to redraw, doctor's orders." Then proceed.
choices.feedback: It gets the blood and gives her nothing. Hiding behind an order when you are the person who knows the reason reads as evasive, and she has the right to know why she is being stuck again.

choices.text: Ask another tech to do the redraw so you do not have to explain.
choices.feedback: Understandable and the wrong instinct. The redraw is yours to do and the explanation is yours to give; handing both off to avoid discomfort is how an error becomes a character issue.

steps.prompt: 0402. Both patients are recollected correctly, labeled at the bedside, scanned, and marked collected at the real times. The charge nurse asks you to complete the safety report. How do you document all of this?

choices.text: Chart the clinical facts in the record (specimens recollected at 0356 and 0400, sites, both patients re-identified, provider and nurses notified) and describe the error fully in the separate safety report, without mentioning the report in the chart.
choices.feedback: Exactly the right split. The medical record carries what happened to the patient; the safety report carries the error analysis, and referencing it in the chart pulls a protected quality document into the legal record.

choices.text: Chart everything, including a note that a safety report was filed about the mislabeling.
choices.feedback: The clinical documentation is right and the last clause is the mistake. 'Incident report filed' in the chart is the sentence that makes a quality document discoverable.

choices.text: File the safety report and leave the chart alone, since the specimens were discarded anyway.
choices.feedback: The chart still needs to show that the patients were redrawn, when, and that the team was notified, because that is care that was delivered. A gap here looks like nothing happened for 40 minutes.

choices.text: Write a detailed narrative in the chart explaining how the labels got switched and that it was your error.
choices.feedback: Honesty is right and the venue is wrong. Root cause analysis belongs in the safety report; the chart records objective clinical facts about the patient, not an investigation of your process.

steps.prompt: 0620. The charge nurse finds you before shift change. "Walk me through how it happened." You know exactly how: you printed both patients' labels at the workstation at the start of the round and carried them in your pocket.

choices.text: Say exactly that, and name the fix: labels print at the bedside printer for one patient at a time, and nothing gets carried in a pocket.
choices.feedback: This is the answer that ends the matter. You identified the mechanism, you are not making excuses, and you have named a specific behavior change rather than promising to be more careful.

choices.text: "It was busy and I got rushed. I'll be more careful."
choices.feedback: True and useless. Being careful is not a system, and every mislabeling event in history happened to someone who intended to be careful. Name the actual mechanism and the actual change.

choices.text: Point out that the label printer near room 3 has been broken for a week, which is why you printed at the workstation.
choices.feedback: A real contributing factor worth reporting, and it does not come first. Lead with what you did and how you will change it, then raise the broken printer as a system issue for the report.

choices.text: Say you are not certain how it happened and that the labels may have been printed wrong.
choices.feedback: You know what happened. Vagueness about a mechanism you can describe reads as concealment and prevents the department from fixing a pattern that is affecting other techs too.

scenarios.debrief:
The pattern to carry: a mislabeled specimen is not a paperwork problem, it is a live clinical hazard until the result is stopped. The order of operations is fixed.

Stop the specimen first. One phone call to the lab, before anything else, because a result that has not posted cannot be acted on. Then tell the humans, in person, starting with whoever might make a decision on that result in the next five minutes. Never relabel; a corrected tube has no verifiable chain of identity and is worth nothing anyway. Then recollect, tell the patient the truth plainly, and file the report.

The documentation split is worth memorizing. The medical record gets the clinical facts: what was recollected, when, from where, who was notified. The safety report gets the error, the sequence, and the contributing factors. Never mention the report inside the chart.

And the mechanism: labels printed in one place and carried to another. Print at the bedside, one patient at a time, label in the room in front of the patient, scan, mark collected. Every step of that workflow exists because of a case like this one.
